Kotlin Multiplatform, from the compiler up · Puzzle 5 · 6 of 16

How Swift sees your Kotlin

In puzzle 0, Kotlin/Native turned your code into native code for the iPhone. But the iOS app is written in Swift. Here's how Swift finds and calls what you built.

Builds on: open one to see the idea this puzzle uses.

  • Puzzle 4: An iOS app in one puzzle

    iOS apps are written in Swift, in Xcode, Apple's IDE. Screens are built with UIKit, Apple's screen framework (or the newer SwiftUI). A view controller manages one screen's UI elements and reacts to the user, much like an Activity or Fragment. Swift looks like Kotlin: let is val, var is var, and a class can subclass UIViewController the way yours subclasses Activity.

Starting from zero? The blocks under this puzzle are 4 puzzles: 0 → 1 → 2 → 4. Know them already? Start here.

The problem

In puzzle 0, Kotlin/Native compiled your shared code to native code for the iPhone. But the iOS app is written in Swift, by a team that may never open a Kotlin file. Native code is just instructions for a CPU: it has no names, no types, no "here's a class called LoginRules". How does Swift know what's in there, and how to call it?

See it

Save this diagram as a GIF

The building block

For iOS, Kotlin/Native packs your shared code into a framework: Apple's format for a library. A framework holds two things: the compiled code, and a description of what's inside, so other code knows what it can call.

That description is a header: a file that lists every class, function and type, without their code. Kotlin writes it in Objective-C, the older language of Apple's platforms, because Swift can call Objective-C directly. Swift has no direct line to Kotlin; it goes through that Objective-C description.

A Gradle task builds the framework (it takes its name from your shared module, often called shared), and the iOS app's project in Xcode, Apple's counterpart of Android Studio, links it in. So the iOS team imports the framework, and in Swift your LoginRules class looks like any other Objective-C class: Swift reads the header and calls the native code behind it.

That middle step has a price. Objective-C is older and simpler than both Kotlin and Swift, so some things don't survive the trip. The next puzzle shows which.

The analogy

A book translated into a third language before it reaches its readers. The readers never see the original; they read the translation. Whatever that third language has no words for gets flattened on the way.

Check yourself

The iOS team opens your framework in Xcode. What do they read to learn your API?

Not quite. Kotlin describes your code in Objective-C, not Swift; Swift reads that.

Not quite. The framework holds native code and an Objective-C description; Swift never reads Kotlin.

Right. Swift learns your API from the Objective-C header.

Why does Kotlin describe your code in Objective-C, not in Swift?

Right. Objective-C is the language Swift already knows how to call.

Not quite. Swift runs native code fine; it needs a description it can read, and Objective-C is one. Re-read that part ↑

What's the difference between a framework and a header?

Not quite. It's the other way round: the header lists, the framework holds the code too.

Not quite. A framework contains the header, plus the compiled code the header describes.

Right. Package vs its description.

  • Kotlin docs: The basics of Kotlin Multiplatform project structure ("When it's built into an iOS framework, common Kotlin is treated as Kotlin/Native")

What you now know

Kotlin/Native packs your shared code into a framework, Apple's format for a library. Its description is an Objective-C header, because Swift can call Objective-C directly; Swift reads that header and calls your Kotlin as if it were Objective-C.
